generation.hypothesis: A newly developed reactive force field that is tuned to the atomistic kinetics of oxide‐scale formation will enable simulations that accurately predict the formation of a dense, protective oxide layer on refractory high‐entropy alloys, thereby guiding the design of alloys with improved oxidation resistance under high‐temperature conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high‐entropy alloys (RHEAs) with unprotected metal surfaces that are prone to degradation in high-temperature, oxidative environments.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a reactive force field using quantum mechanical and atomic-scale simulation techniques specifically calibrated to capture the kinetics of oxide-scale formation on the alloy surface.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation environments (e.g., 1000–1100 °C under oxygen exposure) where oxide scale formation dictates oxidation resistance.
generation.structural_mediator: The simulated formation of a dense and continuous oxide scale that acts as a barrier to further oxidation.
generation.mechanism: The reactive force field captures the atomistic events during oxidation, predicting oxide layer nucleation, growth, and eventual stabilization. This enables assessment of whether the resulting oxide microstructure can serve as an effective barrier against continued oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Simulations will predict oxide-scale formation kinetics that favor the development of a stable, protective layer, correlating with improved oxidation resistance compared to models using standard, non-reactive force fields.
generation.baseline: Current simulation methods or force fields that are not optimized to capture the kinetics of oxide‐scale formation yield less accurate predictions and do not reliably guide protective alloy design.
generation.boundary: The predictions apply to metal/alloy systems in high-temperature oxidative conditions and may vary with alloy composition and experimental specifics.
generation.uncertainty: The exact transferability and quantitative predictive accuracy of the reactive force field remain uncertain until validated against detailed experimental oxidation data.

falsification_experiment.design: Develop the reactive force field and use it in atomistic simulations of oxide-scale formation on a representative RHEA sample. Concurrently, perform high-temperature oxidation experiments on the same alloy under controlled conditions (e.g., 1000–1100 °C). Compare the simulated oxide layer morphology, kinetics (e.g., growth rate), and composition with those obtained from experimental measurements.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and growth rate (via thermogravimetric analysis)
Oxide composition (using X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the simulation results deviate significantly (e.g., more than 20% difference in growth kinetics or mismatches in observed protective oxide phases) from the experimental data, then the reactive force field is not adequately capturing the kinetics of oxide formation and the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Abstract Although refractory high entropy alloys (RHEAs) have shown potentials to be developed as structural materials for elevated temperature applications, most of the reported oxidation behaviours of RHEA were associated with short term exposures for only up to 48 hours, and there is a lack of understanding on the oxidation mechanism of any RHEA to-date. In this work, by using thermogravimetric analysis, isothermal oxidation was conducted on a novel RHEA at 1000 °C and 1100 °C for up to 200 hours, which is an unprecedented testing duration. The external oxide layer strongly influenced the weight gain behaviours, and it consisted of CrTaO 4 -based oxide with some dispersion of Al 2 O 3 and Cr 2 O 3 . At 1000 °C, the inability to form dense CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer resulted an exponential dependence of weight gain throughout 200 hours. At 1100 °C, mass gain curve showed two parabolic dependences associated with the formation of protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer and the weight gain after 200 hours was 4.03 mg/cm 2 , which indicates that it is one of the most oxidation resistant RHEAs comparing to literature data to-date.
